title: Restricting Staff Use of AI Services over Information Protection Concerns: A Comparative Analysis of Three Public Organisations
content: Organisations sometimes restrict their staff's use of an AI service because of information security or personal data concerns. We ask how such decisions differed in their triggering evidence, the reach of the restriction, the workflows affected and the conditions for renewed use. We compare three decisions by public bodies, each documented in official sources and chosen so that their triggers differ: the Dutch central government's interim position on generative AI (2023), the University of Washington's block of the Read AI meeting assistant (2025), and the compliance notice requiring Victoria's Department of Families, Fairness and Housing to block generative AI tools for child-protection staff (2024). We analysed each case against four criteria fixed in advance and recorded each finding, with its source location, in an evidence matrix. Only the Victorian decision followed a confirmed disclosure of personal data; the other two were precautionary. The widest coverage, of tools and of staff, came from the precautionary Dutch decision, which is a policy position; the incident-driven Victorian decision covered one workforce and required technical blocking. The routes back to renewed use differed: conditional approval of use in the Netherlands, vetting of alternative products at Washington, and possible amendment of the regulator's notice in Victoria on evidence of additional controls. With three cases, and sources written by the organisations or the regulator, these findings are patterns to be tested, not general rules.
